claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens can contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Available analytical predictions for HfNbTaTiZr commonly model a perfect, defect-free crystal.
The proposed regression model incorporates descriptors of oxygen-induced lattice distortion, impurity scattering, and temperature-dependent anharmonicity.
The proposed model is trained using both defect-free DFT predictions and experimental conductivity measurements.
Quantum effects and impurity scattering dominate conductivity behavior from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Phonon-phonon interactions and anharmonic effects are significant from approximately 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen produces lattice distortions and defect-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-associated defects modify phonon lifetimes and electron-transport paths.
A model combining theoretical and experimental data can learn the quantitative effects of oxygen and anharmonicity on conductivity.
Machine-learning predictions can be more accurate than conventional analytical predictions.
The proposed model will predict HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Near 100 K, the proposed model will have a significantly smaller prediction error than a perfect-crystal analytical model.
A similar accuracy advantage will occur in the 300–1200 K regime.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions exhibit large conductivity deviations when HfNbTaTiZr contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model is applicable within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
At temperatures outside the specified regimes, very-low-temperature quantum effects or high-temperature phase transformations may require model adjustment.
Machine-learning accuracy depends on the size, composition, quality, and representativeness of the training dataset.
The relative contributions of impurity scattering and anharmonic phonon effects require experimental calibration.
Conductivity should be measured on both low-oxygen and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimens over the two stated temperature ranges.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant error reduction relative to analytical predictions, particularly near 100 K, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The model is declared valid throughout 0–200 K, including temperatures approaching 0 K, but the boundary statement says extreme quantum effects at very low temperatures outside the valid ranges may require adjustment. The lower applicability limit is therefore internally ambiguous.
